reason: With the lids open the cornea takes most of its oxygen from atmospheric oxygen dissolved in the tear film; aqueous supplies the endothelium and becomes the main source only with the eye closed.
Progressive keratoconus in a young adult: corneal cross-linking halts progression; PKP/DALK are reserved for advanced or scarred disease and PRK is contraindicated in ectasia.
Epithelium turns over continuously from limbal stem cells; endothelium essentially does not divide and Bowman layer does not regenerate.
Type I collagen dominates the stroma (with V and VI); type IV is basement membrane, type VII forms anchoring fibrils.
Inferior/inferotemporal steepening (I-S asymmetry) is the earliest topographic sign of keratoconus.
Fleischer ring is iron (hemosiderin) in basal epithelium at the base of the cone, best seen with cobalt blue.
Acute hydrops is stromal imbibition of aqueous after a break in Descemet membrane.

The stem has no explicit question line, but the vignette (contact lens wearer, pain out of proportion, radial keratoneuritis/perineural infiltrates) is pathognomonic for Acanthamoeba, so the key is right. Consider adding 'What is the most likely diagnosis?'
Corneal hysteresis (ORA) is a viscoelastic damping property, i.e. biomechanics, not thickness or curvature.
Posterior elevation and tomographic/pachymetric-progression indices detect subclinical ectasia earlier than refraction, Kmax or CCT alone.
DALK removes stroma down to Descemet membrane and keeps host Descemet and endothelium; DSAEK/DMEK replace them, PKP replaces all layers.
A ring (annular) stromal infiltrate is the classic later sign of Acanthamoeba keratitis.
Stroma is about 90 percent of corneal thickness and its collagen lamellae carry essentially all the tensile load.
The lens placode forms from surface ectoderm induced by the optic vesicle.
PSC sits at the nodal point, so miosis in bright light and glare degrade vision disproportionately; near vision is also reduced.

Key stands because A is the only option that is a cause of PCR at all (wound leak, corneal edema and wrong IOL power are not). Caveat for the explanation: hydrodissection blowout is not really the MOST common cause; most PCRs occur during nuclear phaco or cortical I/A, and hydrodissection rupture is mainly a posterior polar cataract problem.
Corticosteroid cataract is classically posterior subcapsular.
The lens capsule is a thick basement membrane of type IV collagen plus laminin and heparan sulfate proteoglycan.
PCO is by far the most common late complication of cataract surgery.
Hypermature (morgagnian) cataract leaks high-molecular-weight lens protein through an intact capsule; protein and macrophages clog the meshwork: phacolytic glaucoma.
A sharp posterior optic edge blocks lens epithelial cell migration and lowers PCO; hydrophobic acrylic helps too but edge design is the key factor.
ELP prediction is the largest remaining source of error in IOL power formulas.
Pseudoexfoliation weakens zonules (and gives poor dilation); zonular dialysis and capsular complications are the classic intraoperative risk.

No option is embryologically correct. The iris stroma derives from neural crest mesenchyme; the iris pigment epithelium, sphincter and dilator muscles derive from neuroectoderm (anterior rim of the optic cup); iris vascular endothelium is mesodermal. Surface ectoderm contributes nothing to the iris (it gives the lens, corneal and conjunctival epithelium, lid skin and lacrimal gland), so the marked option C ('Surface ectoderm and neural crest cells') is false, and the source's own explanation concedes it picked C only as 'least wrong'. Option C should read 'Neural crest and neuroectoderm' for the item to be answerable.
Blood-aqueous barrier = tight junctions of the non-pigmented ciliary epithelium plus the non-fenestrated iris capillary endothelium.
Posterior synechiae are iris-to-anterior lens capsule adhesions; iris-to-cornea or iris-to-meshwork adhesions are anterior synechiae.

Among the options offered, pigment dispersion syndrome is the classic and most frequent cause of mid-peripheral spoke-like iris transillumination; pseudoexfoliation, the other big cause, is not offered.
Iridodonesis reflects loss of lens support: aphakia, subluxation or dislocation.
A peaked pupil/iris after surgery means iris (or vitreous) incarcerated in the wound, usually with a leak; needs urgent repair.

Loose or broken sutures must be removed promptly (nidus for infection, vascularization and rejection); with 8 intact interrupted sutures the wound is secure at 3 months, so the loose segment is removed and steroid plus antibiotic cover continued. Removing the entire running suture or re-suturing is not required. Note: the stray comment appended to the Q32 explanation ('Both answers A and C could be correct ... I will go with A') belongs to this item and disagrees with the key; C is nevertheless the right choice.
A ring infiltrate in a contact lens wearer failing antibiotics is Acanthamoeba until proven otherwise; scrape for culture/PCR or confocal, and start PHMB or chlorhexidine plus a diamidine.

Cornea verticillata is caused by cationic amphiphilic drugs (amiodarone, chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine, chlorpromazine, indomethacin, tamoxifen) and Fabry disease; sumatriptan is not a cause. Data-quality note: the explanation carries a stray appended comment about PKP sutures that belongs to Q30 and should be removed.

The item is about hyperopic overcorrection after myopic surface ablation, and for steroids the physiology runs the other way. Post-PRK topical corticosteroids suppress keratocyte activation and stromal remodelling, i.e. they PREVENT regression and therefore maintain or worsen a hyperopic result; the standard management of overcorrection is to taper or stop steroids early (and to extend them for undercorrection/regression). Measures used to induce regression in an overcorrected eye are a tight-fitting soft contact lens (hypoxia, edema and epithelial hyperplasia steepen the cornea and produce a myopic shift), topical NSAIDs (reported to promote regression), and, once refraction is stable, hyperopic PRK retreatment. So A, B and C are described treatments and D (topical steroids) is the exception. The explanation's claim that tight lenses are 'flat-fitting' and flatten the cornea is backwards: a tight lens is steep and steepens the cornea, which is exactly why it was used for post-ablation hyperopia.

Two pairs are mismatched as written. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is intrinsically resistant to chloramphenicol (MexAB-OprM efflux), the textbook exception to chloramphenicol's broad spectrum, so B is a genuine mismatch. Amikacin is an aminoglycoside whose cellular uptake needs aerobic metabolism, so it is inactive against the anaerobic Cutibacterium (Propionibacterium) acnes, which is treated with vancomycin, penicillin, cephalosporins or clindamycin, so E is also a mismatch. Syphilis-penicillin and S. aureus-moxifloxacin are correct pairings, and gonorrhea-erythromycin is defensible only as ophthalmia neonatorum prophylaxis (treatment is ceftriaxone). A candidate choosing B would be marked wrong while being right, and the explanation never says why B should be considered matched. Replace either B or E with a correctly matched pair.

Furrow (senile marginal) degeneration is a non-inflammatory, non-progressive thinning in the lucid interval of arcus and needs no treatment; Terrien, Mooren and PUK can all require tectonic surgery or immunosuppression.

Macular dystrophy (keratan sulfate GAG) stains with Alcian blue/colloidal iron; lattice (amyloid) with Congo red; granular (hyaline) with Masson trichrome; Schnyder (lipid) with oil red O. Data-quality note: the stray appended comment about tight contact lenses and NSAIDs belongs to Q33, not this item.
AKC is chronic and perennial, persisting for decades; it is VKC that typically burns out within 5-10 years. The other statements about AKC are true.

Atropine blocks muscarinic (M3) receptors on the lacrimal gland and reduces tearing; pilocarpine and eserine increase it. Timolol can modestly reduce basal tear secretion, but atropine is the intended and best answer.
Thin, irregular or unstable flaps, hyperopic ablations, flap relifts, epithelial defects and prior ingrowth are risk factors; a thick flap is not.

A-C are true, so D is the only candidate. Caveat: cutaneous rosacea does have a female predominance of roughly 2-3:1; the statement is wrong only in the ophthalmic sense that ocular rosacea affects men and women about equally (BCSC 8). Worth rewording to say 'ocular rosacea' explicitly.
Chalazion is a sterile lipogranuloma; antibiotics do nothing. Warm compresses first, then intralesional steroid or incision and curettage.

Keratomalacia needs urgent systemic vitamin A (WHO: 200,000 IU orally on days 1, 2 and 14) plus infection cover; topical retinoids and lubricants are adjuncts only, so D is the false statement. Caveat: statement A ('three stages') is a simplification of the WHO XN/X1A/X1B/X2/X3A/X3B/XS/XF scheme, but D is far more clearly false.
Recurrent ocular HSV presents as blepharoconjunctivitis, epithelial, stromal or endothelial keratitis, and iridocyclitis; episcleritis is not a typical HSV manifestation.

Immunoglobulin and complement ARE bound to the conjunctival epithelium and peripheral cornea in Mooren ulcer, so the 'absence' statement is the false one; suppressor T-cell deficiency, raised IgA and plasma-cell/lymphocyte infiltration are all reported. Data-quality note: the stray appended comment about WHO xerophthalmia stages belongs to Q42.

Dapsone is first-line only for mild to moderate OCP (and contraindicated in G6PD deficiency); severe or rapidly progressive disease needs cyclophosphamide, mycophenolate, rituximab or IVIG. Female 2:1, age over 60 and BMZ IgG/IgA/IgM/C3 deposition are all true.
